title: Ἀχιλλεὺς ἄυπνος· θεῶν ἔρις
titleEn: Sleepless Achilles and the Gods’ Quarrel — Iliad 24.1–92
part: Sleepless Achilles and the Gods’ Quarrel (24.1–92)
about: The assembly at the ships breaks up and the Achaeans think of supper and sleep, but Achilles cannot sleep: he weeps for Patroclus, turns on his bed, walks the shore, and each dawn yokes his horses and drags Hector three times round Patroclus’ mound, while Apollo keeps the body unmarked. For twelve days the gods pity Hector and urge the slayer of Argus to steal him away; Hera, Poseidon and the gleaming-eyed maiden refuse, because of the old hatred for Troy. On the twelfth dawn Apollo reproaches the gods for favouring an Achilles who has lost pity and shame, and Hera answers that Achilles, the son of a goddess, cannot be given the same honour as Hector. Zeus answers that Hector too was dear to the gods and that stealing him is impossible, since Thetis is always with her son; instead he will send for Thetis, to speak a word so that Achilles takes gifts from Priam and releases Hector. Iris dives into the sea like a lead weight, finds Thetis weeping among the sea-goddesses, and calls her to Zeus; Thetis, ashamed to mingle with the gods and full of grief, agrees to go.

sentences.t:
λῦτο δ’ ἀγών, λαοὶ δὲ θοὰς ἐπὶ νῆας ἕκαστοι
ἐσκίδναντ’ ἰέναι.
sentences.l:
And the gathering was loosed, and the people, each to the swift ships,
scattered to go.
sentences.i: The gathering broke up, and the people scattered, each to go to the swift ships.
sentences.n: λῦτο ‘was loosed’ is an aorist without the augment, and ἀγών is ‘the gathering’, the assembly of the funeral games that has just ended in the previous part. λαοί ‘people’ is the subject of ἐσκίδναντ’, an imperfect of σκίδναμαι ‘scatter’, and ἰέναι ‘to go’ is its infinitive; ἕκαστοι ‘each’ is plural because each company goes to its own ships. The unit ends in the middle of line 2.

sentences.t:
τοὶ μὲν δόρποιο μέδοντο
ὕπνου τε γλυκεροῦ ταρπήμεναι·
sentences.l:
They indeed took thought for supper
and to take their fill of sweet sleep;
sentences.i: They turned their thoughts to supper and to taking their fill of sweet sleep;
sentences.n: τοί is the article as a pronoun, ‘they’, and μὲν … αὐτάρ sets the Achaeans against Achilles in the next unit. μέδοντο is an imperfect middle of μέδομαι ‘take thought for’, with δόρποιο ‘supper’ in the genitive; ταρπήμεναι is the aorist passive infinitive of τέρπω, ‘to take one’s fill of’, and takes ὕπνου ‘sleep’ in the genitive. The unit begins in the middle of line 2.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ἀχιλλεὺς
κλαῖε φίλου ἑτάρου μεμνημένος,
sentences.l:
but Achilles
wept, remembering his dear companion,
sentences.i: but Achilles wept as he remembered his dear companion,
sentences.n: κλαῖε ‘wept’ is an imperfect, so the weeping goes on. μεμνημένος is the perfect participle of μιμνῄσκομαι ‘remember’ and takes the genitive φίλου ἑτάρου, ‘dear companion’; ἑτάρου is the Homeric form of ἑταίρου, and the next lines name him as Patroclus. The unit ends in the middle of line 4.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ μιν ὕπνος
ᾕρει πανδαμάτωρ,
sentences.l:
and him sleep did not take,
the all-subduing,
sentences.i: and sleep, which subdues all, did not take him,
sentences.n: ὕπνος ‘sleep’ is the subject, and πανδαμάτωρ ‘all-subduing’ is built from πᾶν ‘all’ and δαμάω ‘subdue’; it stands in apposition to ὕπνος. ᾕρει is an imperfect of αἱρέω ‘take, seize’, with μιν ‘him’ as its object, and οὐδέ means ‘and not’. The unit begins in the middle of line 4 and ends in the middle of line 5.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἐστρέφετ’ ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα
Πατρόκλου ποθέων ἀνδροτῆτά τε καὶ μένος ἠΰ,
sentences.l:
but he turned this way and that,
longing for Patroclus’ manhood and good might,
sentences.i: but he turned this way and that, missing the manhood and the good might of Patroclus,
sentences.n: ἐστρέφετ’ is an imperfect middle of στρέφω ‘turn’, so ‘kept turning himself’, and ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα is ‘this way and that’. ποθέων ‘longing for’ takes two accusatives, ἀνδροτῆτα ‘manhood’ (the quality of being a man) and μένος ‘might’, with ἠΰ ‘good’ agreeing with μένος; Πατρόκλου ‘of Patroclus’ depends on both. Line 6 is metrically irregular as transmitted: the first syllable of ἀνδροτῆτα, closed by ν, would normally be long, but the metre needs it short. The unit begins in the middle of line 5.

sentences.t:
ἠδ’ ὁπόσα τολύπευσε σὺν αὐτῷ καὶ πάθεν ἄλγεα
ἀνδρῶν τε πτολέμους ἀλεγεινά τε κύματα πείρων·
sentences.l:
and all that he wound up along with him, and the pains he suffered,
the wars of men and grievous waves passing through;
sentences.i: and all that he had carried through with him, and the pains he suffered, making his way through the wars of men and the grievous waves;
sentences.n: This clause is a further object of ποθέων in the last unit: Achilles longs for all this as well. ὁπόσα ‘all that’ is the object of τολύπευσε ‘wound up’ (the verb is used of winding wool, and so of bringing a task or a war to its end), and πάθεν is the aorist ‘suffered’ with ἄλγεα ‘pains’. The verbs have no stated subject; the sentence has been about Achilles, so ‘he’ is Achilles and αὐτῷ ‘him’ is Patroclus, though the Greek alone would allow the reverse. πείρων ‘passing through’ is a nominative participle of the same subject; its second line, ἀνδρῶν τε πτολέμους ἀλεγεινά τε κύματα πείρων, also stands in the Odyssey, there said by the speaker of himself.

sentences.t: τῶν μιμνησκόμενος θαλερὸν κατὰ δάκρυον εἶβεν,
sentences.l: of these remembering, an abundant tear down he let fall,
sentences.i: As he remembered all this, he let abundant tears fall,
sentences.n: τῶν ‘of these things’ is the genitive after μιμνησκόμενος ‘remembering’, and κατά … εἶβεν is a split verb (tmesis) for κατείβω ‘let fall down’; εἶβεν is an imperfect, so the tears kept falling. θαλερὸν δάκρυον is ‘an abundant tear’, singular in the Greek.

sentences.t:
ἄλλοτ’ ἐπὶ πλευρὰς κατακείμενος, ἄλλοτε δ’ αὖτε
ὕπτιος, ἄλλοτε δὲ πρηνής·
sentences.l:
At one time lying on his sides, at another again
on his back, and at another on his face;
sentences.i: At one time he lay on his side, at another on his back, at another face down;
sentences.n: ἄλλοτ’ … ἄλλοτε … ἄλλοτε is ‘at one time … at another … at another’, and αὖτε ‘again’ adds nothing to the count. κατακείμενος ‘lying’ is a participle belonging to Achilles, and ὕπτιος ‘on his back’ and πρηνής ‘on his face’ are adjectives with the same understood ‘lying’; ἐπὶ πλευράς ‘onto his sides’ is plural in the Greek. The unit ends in the middle of line 11.

sentences.t:
τοτὲ δ’ ὀρθὸς ἀναστὰς
δινεύεσκ’ ἀλύων παρὰ θῖν’ ἁλός·
sentences.l:
then upright, having risen up,
he would go wheeling about, distraught, along the shore of the sea;
sentences.i: then he would rise upright and wheel about, distraught, along the shore of the sea;
sentences.n: τοτὲ δ’ ‘and then’ continues the series from the last unit. δινεύεσκ’ is an iterative imperfect (the -σκ- ending means ‘used to, would’) of δινεύω ‘wheel about’, and ἀλύων ‘distraught’ describes his state; ὀρθὸς ἀναστάς is ‘upright, having risen’. παρὰ θῖν’ ἁλός is ‘along the shore of the sea’, θῖν’ being θῖνα with the final vowel elided. The unit begins in the middle of line 11 and ends in the middle of line 12.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ μιν ἠὼς
φαινομένη λήθεσκεν ὑπεὶρ ἅλα τ’ ἠϊόνας τε.
sentences.l:
and him the dawn
appearing did not escape, over the sea and the beaches.
sentences.i: and the dawn, as it appeared over the sea and the beaches, never escaped his notice.
sentences.n: λήθεσκεν is an iterative imperfect of λήθω, here with the accusative μιν ‘him’, so it means ‘escaped the notice of him’; ἠώς is ‘dawn’, and φαινομένη ‘appearing’ agrees with it. ὑπεὶρ is ὑπέρ ‘over’, ἅλα is ‘sea’, and ἠϊόνας ‘beaches’ is plural. The unit begins in the middle of line 12.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅ γ’ ἐπεὶ ζεύξειεν ὑφ’ ἅρμασιν ὠκέας ἵππους,
Ἕκτορα δ’ ἕλκεσθαι δησάσκετο δίφρου ὄπισθεν,
sentences.l:
But he, whenever he had yoked the swift horses under the chariot,
would bind Hector to be dragged behind the chariot,
sentences.i: But whenever he had yoked the swift horses to the chariot, he would tie Hector on to be dragged behind the chariot,
sentences.n: ἐπεὶ ζεύξειεν is ‘whenever he had yoked’: ἐπεί with an optative and no ἄν describes a repeated action in the past, and the main verb δησάσκετο is an iterative aorist middle of δέω ‘bind’ with the same sense, ‘would bind’. ὑφ’ ἅρμασιν is ‘under the chariot’, the horses being put to it. ἕλκεσθαι is a passive infinitive of purpose, ‘to be dragged’, and δίφρου ὄπισθεν is ‘behind the chariot’, the genitive after ὄπισθεν; δίφρος is the chariot’s board here; the same word means a stool in another setting.

sentences.t:
τρὶς δ’ ἐρύσας περὶ σῆμα Μενοιτιάδαο θανόντος
αὖτις ἐνὶ κλισίῃ παυέσκετο,
sentences.l:
and three times having dragged him round the tomb of the dead son of Menoetius,
again in the hut he would rest,
sentences.i: and when he had dragged him three times round the tomb of the dead son of Menoetius, he would stop and rest again in his hut,
sentences.n: τρίς ‘three times’ and ἐρύσας ‘having dragged’ (aorist participle) have Hector as an understood object from the last unit. Μενοιτιάδαο θανόντος is ‘of the dead son of Menoetius’, the patronymic of Patroclus, with θανόντος ‘having died’ agreeing with it; σῆμα is ‘tomb’. παυέσκετο is an iterative imperfect middle of παύω, ‘would stop’, and κλισίῃ is ‘hut’. The unit begins at the start of line 16 and ends in the middle of line 17.

sentences.t:
τὸν δέ τ’ ἔασκεν
ἐν κόνι ἐκτανύσας προπρηνέα·
sentences.l:
and him he would leave,
having stretched him out in the dust, face down;
sentences.i: and he would leave him stretched out face down in the dust;
sentences.n: τὸν is the article as a pronoun, ‘him’, Hector, and τε is a connecting particle. ἔασκεν is an iterative imperfect of ἐάω ‘let be, leave’, and προπρηνέα ‘face down’ agrees with τὸν, while ἐκτανύσας ‘having stretched out’ is a nominative participle that goes with the subject, Achilles. κόνις is ‘dust’. The unit begins and ends in the middle of lines.

sentences.t:
τοῖο δ’ Ἀπόλλων
πᾶσαν ἀεικείην ἄπεχε χροῒ φῶτ’ ἐλεαίρων
καὶ τεθνηότα περ·
sentences.i: but Apollo kept all unseemly treatment from his skin, pitying the man even though he was dead;
sentences.n: τοῖο is ‘of him’, Hector’s, and goes with χροῒ, the dative of χρώς ‘skin’; ἄπεχε ‘kept off’ is an imperfect, with πᾶσαν ἀεικείην ‘all unseemly treatment’ as its object (ἀεικής is ‘unseemly’). φῶτ’ is φῶτα ‘man’, and ἐλεαίρων ‘pitying’ is Apollo’s motive; τεθνηότα περ ‘though dead’ is a perfect participle with the concessive particle. The unit begins in the middle of line 18 and ends in the middle of line 20.

sentences.t:
περὶ δ’ αἰγίδι πάντα κάλυπτε
χρυσείῃ, ἵνα μή μιν ἀποδρύφοι ἑλκυστάζων.
sentences.l:
and all of him with the aegis he covered about,
the golden one, so that he should not tear him, as he dragged him about.
sentences.i: and covered all of him round with the golden aegis, so that Achilles, dragging him about, should not tear him.
sentences.n: περὶ … κάλυπτε is a split verb (tmesis), ‘covered round’, and πάντα ‘all of him’ is its object; αἰγίδι is the dative ‘with the aegis’, and χρυσείῃ ‘golden’ agrees with it from the next line. ἵνα μή with the optative ἀποδρύφοι says what is to be avoided: ἀποδρύπτω is ‘tear off, tear away’, and the Greek gives only μιν ‘him’ as its object, not what is torn. ἑλκυστάζων is ‘dragging about’, a repeated dragging, and Achilles is the subject of ἀποδρύφοι and ἑλκυστάζων, while Apollo is the subject of κάλυπτε.

sentences.t: ὣς ὃ μὲν Ἕκτορα δῖον ἀείκιζεν μενεαίνων·
sentences.l: So he, on the one hand, was treating heavenly Hector unseemly, in eagerness;
sentences.i: So he ill-treated heavenly Hector in his eagerness;
sentences.n: ὣς ὃ μὲν rounds off the last scene, ‘so he, for his part’, Achilles, and sets it against the gods in the next lines. ἀείκιζεν is an imperfect of ἀεικίζω ‘treat in an unseemly way’, from ἀεικής ‘unseemly’, and Ἕκτορα δῖον is ‘heavenly Hector’. μενεαίνων ‘in eagerness’ is a participle that says he was straining at it; the Greek does not name the feeling, and the anger is for the reader to supply.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἐλεαίρεσκον μάκαρες θεοὶ εἰσορόωντες,
sentences.l: but him pitied the blessed gods, looking on,
sentences.i: but the blessed gods, looking on, kept pitying him,
sentences.n: ἐλεαίρεσκον is an iterative imperfect of ἐλεαίρω ‘pity’, with τὸν ‘him’ (Hector) as its object, so the pity returns again and again; μάκαρες θεοί are ‘the blessed gods’, and εἰσορόωντες ‘looking on’ is a participle agreeing with them.

sentences.t: κλέψαι δ’ ὀτρύνεσκον ἐΰσκοπον ἀργεϊφόντην.
sentences.l: and they kept urging the keen-sighted Argeïphontes to steal him.
sentences.i: and they kept urging the keen-sighted slayer of Argus to steal him away.
sentences.n: κλέψαι ‘to steal’ is an aorist infinitive after ὀτρύνεσκον ‘kept urging’, an iterative imperfect; ‘him’ (Hector) is understood. ἐΰσκοπον ‘keen-sighted’ and ἀργεϊφόντην ‘Argeïphontes’ are two accusatives naming Hermes without naming him; ‘slayer of Argus’ is the usual explanation of ἀργεϊφόντης, but the word’s meaning is disputed.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἄλλοις μὲν πᾶσιν ἑήνδανεν, οὐδέ ποθ’ Ἥρῃ
οὐδὲ Ποσειδάων’ οὐδὲ γλαυκώπιδι κούρῃ,
sentences.l:
Then to all the others it was pleasing, but never to Hera,
nor to Poseidon, nor to the gleaming-eyed maiden,
sentences.i: That pleased all the others, but never Hera, nor Poseidon, nor the gleaming-eyed maiden,
sentences.n: The subject of ἑήνδανεν ‘it was pleasing’ is the plan to steal Hector, left unstated; it is an imperfect of ἁνδάνω ‘please’ with an unusual augmented form, and takes a dative, here ἄλλοις … πᾶσιν ‘all the others’ and Ἥρῃ. Ποσειδάων’ is elided, and goes in the same construction as Ἥρῃ; the elision hides its ending. γλαυκώπιδι κούρῃ is ‘the gleaming-eyed maiden’, Athena unnamed, and ποθ’ is ποτέ ‘ever’, so οὐδέ ποθ’ means ‘and never’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἔχον ὥς σφιν πρῶτον ἀπήχθετο Ἴλιος ἱρὴ
καὶ Πρίαμος καὶ λαὸς Ἀλεξάνδρου ἕνεκ’ ἄτης,
sentences.l:
but they held fast, as when first sacred Ilium had become hateful to them,
and Priam and the people, on account of Alexander’s bewilderment;
sentences.i: but they held firm, as from the first, when sacred Ilium and Priam and his people became hateful to them, because of Alexander’s bewilderment;
sentences.n: ἔχον ‘they held’ has no object in the Greek; the sense is that Hera, Poseidon and Athena kept to their hostility. ὥς … πρῶτον ἀπήχθετο is ‘as when first it became hateful’, an aorist of ἀπέχθομαι, with three subjects, Ἴλιος ἱρή ‘sacred Ilium’, Πρίαμος and λαός ‘people’, and σφιν ‘to them’ means those three, Hera, Poseidon and Athena. Ἀλεξάνδρου is Paris, ‘of Alexander’, and ἄτη ‘bewilderment’ is the clouding of his mind that made him do wrong; ἕνεκ’ means ‘on account of’.

sentences.t: ὃς νείκεσσε θεὰς ὅτε οἱ μέσσαυλον ἵκοντο,
sentences.l: who reviled the goddesses when they came to his mid-yard,
sentences.i: who reviled the goddesses when they came to his farmyard,
sentences.n: ὅς ‘who’ is Alexander again. νείκεσσε is an aorist of νεικέω ‘revile’, and θεάς ‘goddesses’ is its object; the Greek does not say which two, and the next line names the third by what she gave. μέσσαυλον is ‘mid-yard’, the open space in the middle of the steading, and οἱ is ‘to him’ with ἵκοντο ‘they came’, an aorist of ἱκνέομαι.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ᾔνησ’ ἥ οἱ πόρε μαχλοσύνην ἀλεγεινήν.
sentences.l: and praised the one who gave him grievous lust.
sentences.i: and praised the one who gave him grievous lust.
sentences.n: τὴν ‘her’ is the goddess he praised, antecedent to ἥ ‘who’, and the Greek does not name her. ᾔνησ’ is an aorist of αἰνέω ‘praise’, and πόρε ‘gave’ is an aorist without the augment, with οἱ ‘to him’. μαχλοσύνη ‘lust’ is a rare word for unrestrained desire, and ἀλεγεινήν ‘grievous’ agrees with it.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δή ῥ’ ἐκ τοῖο δυωδεκάτη γένετ’ ἠώς,
καὶ τότ’ ἄρ’ ἀθανάτοισι μετηύδα Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων·
sentences.l:
But when from that time the twelfth dawn came to be,
and then indeed among the immortals spoke Phoebus Apollo:
sentences.i: But when the twelfth dawn had come after that day, then Phoebus Apollo spoke among the immortals:
sentences.n: The first line is the same line as 1.493, and ἐκ τοῖο ‘from that’ reaches back to the time of the events just told; the Greek does not say which day is counted as the first. δυωδεκάτη ‘twelfth’ agrees with ἠώς ‘dawn’, and μετηύδα ‘spoke among’ takes the dative ἀθανάτοισι ‘immortals’; καὶ τότ’ ἄρ’ is ‘and then, you see’. The colon introduces Apollo’s speech, which runs to 54.

sentences.t: σχέτλιοί ἐστε θεοί, δηλήμονες·
sentences.l: “Cruel ones you are, gods, hurtful;
sentences.i: “You are cruel, you gods, and hurtful;
sentences.n: ἐστε ‘you are’ takes σχέτλιοι ‘cruel ones’ as predicate, and θεοί is ‘gods’, the address; δηλήμονες ‘hurtful’ comes from δηλέομαι ‘hurt’ and is a second predicate. The opening quotation mark begins Apollo’s speech, which runs to 54.

sentences.t:
οὔ νύ ποθ’ ὑμῖν
Ἕκτωρ μηρί’ ἔκηε βοῶν αἰγῶν τε τελείων;
sentences.l:
did not, then, ever, for you,
Hector burn thigh-pieces of oxen and of unblemished goats?
sentences.i: Did Hector never burn thigh-pieces for you, of oxen and of goats without blemish?
sentences.n: οὔ νύ ποθ’ ‘did not … ever’ opens a question that expects the answer yes. ἔκηε is an aorist of καίω ‘burn’, and μηρία ‘thigh-pieces’ (elided to μηρί’) are the fat-wrapped thighs burnt for the gods; βοῶν αἰγῶν τε ‘of oxen and of goats’ are genitives depending on them. τελείων ‘unblemished’ agrees with both; a victim was τέλειος ‘perfect, complete’. The unit begins in the middle of line 33.

sentences.t:
τὸν νῦν οὐκ ἔτλητε νέκυν περ ἐόντα σαῶσαι
ᾗ τ’ ἀλόχῳ ἰδέειν καὶ μητέρι καὶ τέκεϊ ᾧ
καὶ πατέρι Πριάμῳ λαοῖσί τε,
sentences.i: Him you could not now bring yourselves to save, corpse though he is, for his wife to look on, and his mother and his child, and his father Priam, and the people,
sentences.n: τὸν ‘him’ is Hector, the object of σαῶσαι ‘to save’, an aorist infinitive after ἔτλητε ‘you have endured’ (from τλάω ‘endure’, the same verb as τλητόν in 49). νέκυν περ ἐόντα is ‘corpse though being’. ἰδέειν ‘to see’ is a second infinitive with all the datives as its subjects: ᾗ τ’ ἀλόχῳ ‘his own wife’, μητέρι, τέκεϊ ᾧ ‘his own child’, πατέρι Πριάμῳ and λαοῖσι.

sentences.t:
τοί κέ μιν ὦκα
ἐν πυρὶ κήαιεν καὶ ἐπὶ κτέρεα κτερίσαιεν.
sentences.l:
who would quickly
burn him in a fire and render funeral rites over him.
sentences.i: who would quickly burn him in the fire and pay him funeral honours.
sentences.n: τοί ‘they’ picks up all the persons named in the last unit, and with κε and the optative it says ‘they who would’. κήαιεν is an aorist optative of καίω ‘burn’. κτέρεα … κτερίσαιεν is a figure of the verb and its own noun: κτέρεα are the goods or honours given to the dead, and κτερίζω is ‘pay these rites’; the English gives the pair as one phrase, and ἐπί goes with the verb, ‘over him’. The unit begins in the middle of line 37.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ὀλοῷ Ἀχιλῆϊ θεοὶ βούλεσθ’ ἐπαρήγειν,
sentences.l: But deadly Achilles you gods wish to help,
sentences.i: but it is deadly Achilles whom you gods wish to help,
sentences.n: ὀλοῷ ‘deadly’ agrees with Ἀχιλῆϊ, and the dative is the object of ἐπαρήγειν ‘to help’; βούλεσθ’ is βούλεσθε ‘you wish’, with the last vowel elided.

sentences.t:
ᾧ οὔτ’ ἂρ φρένες εἰσὶν ἐναίσιμοι οὔτε νόημα
γναμπτὸν ἐνὶ στήθεσσι,
sentences.l:
in whom there are neither wits that are fitting nor a mind
that bends within his chest,
sentences.i: in whom there are no fitting wits, and no mind that can bend in his chest,
sentences.n: ᾧ ‘in whom’ is a dative of possession, ‘to whom’, and the clause says what Achilles lacks: φρένες ἐναίσιμοι ‘fitting wits’ and νόημα γναμπτόν ‘a mind that bends’, which is the same as a flexible one; οὔτε … οὔτε is ‘neither … nor’, and ἂρ is ἄρα. The unit begins at the start of line 40 and ends in the middle of line 41.

sentences.t: λέων δ’ ὣς ἄγρια οἶδεν,
sentences.l: and like a lion he knows savage things,
sentences.i: and he knows savage things, like a lion,
sentences.n: οἶδεν ‘he knows’ is a perfect in form and a present in sense, and ἄγρια ‘savage things’ is the object; λέων is ‘lion’ and ὥς ‘as’, so the comparison is ‘as a lion’ (the lion is a nominative, not the object). The unit begins in the middle of line 41, and the lion carries the comparison into the next unit.

sentences.t:
ὅς τ’ ἐπεὶ ἂρ μεγάλῃ τε βίῃ καὶ ἀγήνορι θυμῷ
εἴξας εἶσ’ ἐπὶ μῆλα βροτῶν ἵνα δαῖτα λάβῃσιν·
sentences.l:
who, when to great might and manly spirit
having yielded, goes against the flocks of mortals, to get a feast;
sentences.i: who, once he has yielded to his great might and proud spirit, goes after the flocks of men to get a feast;
sentences.n: The unit continues the lion: ὅς τ’ ‘who’ is the lion, with a generalizing τε. εἴξας is the aorist participle of εἴκω ‘yield’ and takes the dative μεγάλῃ … βίῃ καὶ ἀγήνορι θυμῷ, ‘great might and manly spirit’; εἶσ’ is εἶσι ‘goes’, with ἐπὶ μῆλα ‘to the flocks’. βροτῶν is ‘of mortals’, and ἵνα with the subjunctive δαῖτα λάβῃσιν says ‘in order to take a feast’.

sentences.t: ὣς Ἀχιλεὺς ἔλεον μὲν ἀπώλεσεν,
sentences.l: so Achilles has destroyed pity,
sentences.i: so Achilles has lost all pity,
sentences.n: ὣς ‘so’ closes the comparison and is followed by the application to Achilles. ἔλεον ‘pity’ is the object of ἀπώλεσεν, an aorist of ἀπόλλυμι ‘destroy, lose’; μὲν looks forward to the next unit. The unit ends in the middle of line 44.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ οἱ αἰδὼς
γίγνεται, ἥ τ’ ἄνδρας μέγα σίνεται ἠδ’ ὀνίνησι.
sentences.l:
and shame does not come to him,
which greatly harms men and also helps them.
sentences.i: and shame does not come to him, shame that does men great harm and also good.
sentences.n: οὐδέ οἱ ‘and not to him’ goes with γίγνεται ‘comes to be’. αἰδώς ‘shame’ is the sense of restraint that stops a man from wrong, and it can also mean ‘respect’; ἥ τ’ ‘which’ has a generalizing τε. σίνεται ‘harms’ and ὀνίνησι ‘helps’ are both present, with ἄνδρας ‘men’ as the object of the first and μέγα ‘greatly’ with it. The unit begins in the middle of line 44.

sentences.t:
μέλλει μέν πού τις καὶ φίλτερον ἄλλον ὀλέσσαι
ἠὲ κασίγνητον ὁμογάστριον ἠὲ καὶ υἱόν·
sentences.l:
A man, I suppose, is bound to lose even another who is dearer,
either a brother of the same womb, or even a son;
sentences.i: Some man, I suppose, is bound to lose someone even dearer, a brother of the same womb or a son;
sentences.n: μέλλει ‘is bound to’ takes the aorist infinitive ὀλέσσαι ‘to lose’; πού ‘I suppose’ softens it, and τις is ‘some man’. καὶ φίλτερον ἄλλον ‘even another, dearer’ gives no ‘than’, so the comparison is left open, though the context points to Patroclus. κασίγνητον ὁμογάστριον is ‘a brother of the same belly’, that is, of the same mother, and ἠέ … ἠέ is ‘either … or’.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἤτοι κλαύσας καὶ ὀδυράμενος μεθέηκε·
sentences.l: but truly, having wept and lamented, he has let it go;
sentences.i: but then, once he has wept and lamented, he lets it go;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἤτοι ‘but truly’; ἤτοι is printed as one word, as in the edition. κλαύσας and ὀδυράμενος are aorist participles, ‘having wept and lamented’, and μεθέηκε is an aorist of μεθίημι ‘let go’ in a general statement, so ‘lets go’; it has no object, and what he lets go is the grief.

sentences.t: τλητὸν γὰρ Μοῖραι θυμὸν θέσαν ἀνθρώποισιν.
sentences.l: for an enduring heart the Fates have put in men.
sentences.i: for the Fates have given men an enduring heart.
sentences.n: τλητόν ‘enduring’ comes from τλάω ‘endure’, the same verb as ἔτλητε in 35, and agrees with θυμόν ‘heart’. θέσαν is an aorist of τίθημι ‘put, set’ without the augment, and Μοῖραι ‘Fates’ are the subject.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὅ γ’ Ἕκτορα δῖον, ἐπεὶ φίλον ἦτορ ἀπηύρα,
ἵππων ἐξάπτων περὶ σῆμ’ ἑτάροιο φίλοιο
ἕλκει·
sentences.i: But he, when he has taken the life from heavenly Hector, fastens him to his horses and drags him round the tomb of his dear companion;
sentences.n: ὅ γ’ ‘he’ is Achilles again. ἀπηύρα is an aorist of ἀπαυράω ‘take away’ with two accusatives, Ἕκτορα as the person and φίλον ἦτορ ‘dear heart’ as the thing; ἦτορ is the heart as the seat of life. ἐξάπτων ‘fastening’ takes ἵππων in the genitive, ‘to the horses’; σῆμ’ is σῆμα ‘tomb’ and ἑτάροιο φίλοιο is ‘of his dear companion’. ἕλκει ‘drags’ is present, and the present tense is used for the habit that the poem has just described as repeated. The unit ends in the middle of line 52.

sentences.t: οὐ μήν οἱ τό γε κάλλιον οὐδέ τ’ ἄμεινον.
sentences.l: But that, certainly, is neither finer nor better for him.
sentences.i: But that is neither finer nor better for him.
sentences.n: οὐ μήν ‘but surely not’; οἱ is ‘for him’, the dative of interest, and τό γε ‘that, at least’ is the dragging. κάλλιον ‘finer’ and ἄμεινον ‘better’ are both comparatives, and the Greek supplies no verb. The unit begins in the middle of line 52.

sentences.t: μὴ ἀγαθῷ περ ἐόντι νεμεσσηθέωμέν οἱ ἡμεῖς·
sentences.l: Let us not, we ourselves, feel resentment against him, good man though he is;
sentences.i: Let us not feel resentment against him, good man though he is;
sentences.n: μὴ … νεμεσσηθέωμεν is a first-person plural prohibition, ‘let us not feel resentment’, with οἱ ‘against him’ in the dative; νεμεσσάω is to feel righteous indignation. ἀγαθῷ περ ἐόντι ‘though he is good’ is a dative participle phrase agreeing with οἱ, and ἡμεῖς ‘we’ is an emphatic extra. The reason follows in 54 with γάρ.

sentences.t: κωφὴν γὰρ δὴ γαῖαν ἀεικίζει μενεαίνων.
sentences.l: for he is, indeed, treating the deaf earth unseemly, in eagerness.”
sentences.i: for in his eagerness he is ill-treating the senseless earth.”
sentences.n: γὰρ δή ‘for indeed’ gives the reason for 53. κωφὴν ‘deaf, dull’ agrees with γαῖαν ‘earth’, which most readers take as Hector’s dead body, though the Greek says only ‘earth’; ἀεικίζει and μενεαίνων are the words of line 22, here with the earth as the object. The closing quotation mark ends Apollo’s speech, which began at 33.

sentences.t: τὸν δὲ χολωσαμένη προσέφη λευκώλενος Ἥρη·
sentences.l: And him, enraged, white-armed Hera addressed:
sentences.i: Then white-armed Hera, enraged, said to him:
sentences.n: τὸν δὲ ‘and him’ is Apollo, and χολωσαμένη is the aorist participle of χολόω ‘make angry’ in the middle, ‘having become enraged’; προσέφη is ‘addressed’, the aorist that introduces a speech. λευκώλενος ‘white-armed’ is Hera’s stock epithet. The colon opens her speech, which runs to 63.

sentences.t:
εἴη κεν καὶ τοῦτο τεὸν ἔπος ἀργυρότοξε
εἰ δὴ ὁμὴν Ἀχιλῆϊ καὶ Ἕκτορι θήσετε τιμήν.
sentences.l:
“This too might be your word, silver-bowed one,
if indeed you will set the same honour on Achilles and on Hector.
sentences.i: “This too might be a word of yours, silver-bowed one, if you gods really will give Achilles and Hector the same honour.
sentences.n: εἴη κεν ‘might be’ is an optative of possibility, with τοῦτο … ἔπος ‘this word’ as its subject and τεὸν ‘your’ agreeing with it; the Greek does not say whether it might be right or only fitting. ἀργυρότοξε ‘silver-bowed one’ is the vocative, Apollo. θήσετε ‘you will put’ is a plural future (the gods together), with ὁμὴν … τιμήν ‘the same honour’ and the datives Ἀχιλῆϊ and Ἕκτορι.

sentences.t: Ἕκτωρ μὲν θνητός τε γυναῖκά τε θήσατο μαζόν·
sentences.l: Hector was subject to death, and drew a woman’s breast;
sentences.i: Hector was subject to death, and he sucked a woman’s breast;
sentences.n: θνητός ‘subject to death’ and the τε … τε ‘both … and’ make Hector both mortal and nursed; it is a predicate adjective, and θήσατο is the aorist middle of θῆσθαι ‘suckle’, with μαζόν ‘breast’ as its object and γυναῖκα ‘woman’ as a second accusative; the English takes them together, ‘a woman’s breast’. Hera’s point is that Hector was an ordinary nursed child. μὲν looks forward to αὐτάρ in the next line.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ἀχιλλεύς ἐστι θεᾶς γόνος, ἣν ἐγὼ αὐτὴ
θρέψά τε καὶ ἀτίτηλα καὶ ἀνδρὶ πόρον παράκοιτιν
Πηλέϊ,
sentences.l:
but Achilles is the offspring of a goddess, whom I myself
reared and fostered, and gave as consort to a man,
to Peleus,
sentences.i: but Achilles is the son of a goddess, whom I myself reared and fostered, and gave as wife to a man, to Peleus,
sentences.n: γόνος ‘offspring’ is the predicate noun after ἐστι, with Ἀχιλλεύς as subject, and has θεᾶς ‘of a goddess’, Thetis. ἣν ἐγὼ αὐτὴ ‘whom I myself’ starts a relative clause with θρέψα ‘reared’, ἀτίτηλα ‘fostered’ (an aorist of ἀτιτάλλω), and πόρον ‘I gave’; παράκοιτιν ‘consort’ is the bedfellow, here ‘wife’, and Πηλέϊ is the dative ‘to Peleus’. The unit ends in the middle of line 61.

sentences.t: ὃς περὶ κῆρι φίλος γένετ’ ἀθανάτοισι.
sentences.l: who exceedingly, in heart, became dear to the immortals.
sentences.i: who became exceedingly dear in the hearts of the immortals.
sentences.n: ὃς is Peleus. περί here is the adverb ‘exceedingly’, and κῆρι ‘in heart’ is a dative of κῆρ, with φίλος ‘dear’ and ἀθανάτοισι ‘to the immortals’; γένετ’ is the aorist ‘became’. The unit begins in the middle of line 61.

sentences.t: πάντες δ’ ἀντιάασθε θεοὶ γάμου·
sentences.l: And you all, gods, came to the wedding;
sentences.i: And you gods all came to the wedding;
sentences.n: ἀντιάασθε is a second-person plural middle of ἀντιάω ‘meet, take part in’, with γάμου ‘wedding’ in the genitive; the sense is past, recalling the wedding of Peleus and Thetis, and the form has no augment. πάντες θεοί ‘all the gods’ is the subject. The unit ends in the middle of line 62.

sentences.t:
ἐν δὲ σὺ τοῖσι
δαίνυ’ ἔχων φόρμιγγα κακῶν ἕταρ’, αἰὲν ἄπιστε.
sentences.l:
and among them you
feasted, holding the lyre, companion of evil ones, ever faithless.”
sentences.i: and among them you feasted, with your lyre, companion of evil ones, ever faithless.”
sentences.n: ἐν … τοῖσι is ‘among them’, the gods at the wedding, and σὺ ‘you’ is Apollo; δαίνυ’ is δαίνυο, the imperfect middle of δαίνυμι ‘feast’ with the last vowel elided, and φόρμιγγα is ‘lyre’. κακῶν ἕταρ’ is a vocative, ‘companion of evil ones’, with the genitive plural of κακός; the Greek does not say whether men or things are meant. αἰὲν ἄπιστε ‘ever faithless’ is a second vocative, ἄπιστος being ‘not to be trusted’. The closing quotation mark ends Hera’s speech. The unit begins in the middle of line 62, and its last line ends the speech.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη νεφεληγερέτα Ζεύς·
sentences.l: Her answering addressed cloud-gatherer Zeus:
sentences.i: In answer Zeus who gathers the clouds said to her:
sentences.n: A line used again and again for Zeus answering: τὴν ‘her’ is Hera, ἀπαμειβόμενος ‘answering’ is the participle of ἀπαμείβομαι, and προσέφη is the aorist ‘addressed’. νεφεληγερέτα is ‘cloud-gatherer’, Zeus’s stock epithet, here translated as ‘who gathers the clouds’ in the English. The colon opens Zeus’s speech, which runs to 76.

sentences.t: Ἥρη μὴ δὴ πάμπαν ἀποσκύδμαινε θεοῖσιν·
sentences.l: “Hera, do not now be altogether angry with the gods;
sentences.i: “Hera, do not be so utterly angry with the gods;
sentences.n: μὴ with the imperative ἀποσκύδμαινε is a prohibition, ‘do not be’; σκυδμαίνω is ‘be angry, sullen’ and ἀπο- adds ‘away’, so the English keeps only the anger. δή ‘now, indeed’ and πάμπαν ‘altogether’ strengthen it, and θεοῖσιν is ‘with the gods’, in the dative.

sentences.t: οὐ μὲν γὰρ τιμή γε μί’ ἔσσεται·
sentences.l: for honour will not, indeed, be one;
sentences.i: for honour will not be one and the same;
sentences.n: οὐ μὲν γὰρ is ‘for surely not’. τιμή ‘honour’ is the subject, and μί’ is μία ‘one’ elided, so the clause says honour will not be a single, equal thing; it picks up ὁμὴν … τιμήν ‘the same honour’ in 57. γε is a particle that adds emphasis, and the unit ends in the middle of line 66.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ καὶ Ἕκτωρ
φίλτατος ἔσκε θεοῖσι βροτῶν οἳ ἐν Ἰλίῳ εἰσίν·
sentences.l:
but Hector too
was dearest to the gods of mortals who are in Ilium;
sentences.i: but Hector too was the dearest to the gods of all mortals who are in Ilium;
sentences.n: ἀλλὰ καὶ Ἕκτωρ ‘but Hector also’ answers Hera’s case for Achilles. ἔσκε is ‘was’, an iterative form of εἰμί, and φίλτατος ‘dearest’ is the superlative of φίλος; βροτῶν οἳ ἐν Ἰλίῳ εἰσίν is a partitive genitive, ‘of the mortals who are in Ilium’, and θεοῖσι is ‘to the gods’. The unit begins in the middle of line 66.

sentences.t:
ὣς γὰρ ἔμοιγ’, ἐπεὶ οὔ τι φίλων ἡμάρτανε δώρων.
οὐ γάρ μοί ποτε βωμὸς ἐδεύετο δαιτὸς ἐΐσης
λοιβῆς τε κνίσης τε· τὸ γὰρ λάχομεν γέρας ἡμεῖς.
sentences.l:
For so to me, at least, he was, since he never missed dear gifts.
For never did my altar lack the equal feast,
libation and savour; for that is the prize we have received by lot, we ourselves.
sentences.i: For he was that to me, at least, since he never failed in dear gifts. For my altar has never gone short of the equally shared feast, the libation and the savour; that is the prize of honour we gods have received.
sentences.n: ὣς ‘so’ stands for the superlative of the last line, ‘dearest’, and ἔμοιγ’ is ‘to me, at least’. ἡμάρτανε is an imperfect of ἁμαρτάνω ‘miss, fail’, with φίλων δώρων ‘dear gifts’ in the genitive. Lines 69–70 are the same as 4.48–49, said there too by Zeus: ἐδεύετο is ‘lacked’, and takes the genitives δαιτὸς ἐΐσης ‘the equal feast’, λοιβῆς ‘libation’ and κνίσης ‘savour’; τὸ γὰρ λάχομεν γέρας ἡμεῖς is ‘for that is the prize we have received by lot’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἤτοι κλέψαι μὲν ἐάσομεν, οὐδέ πῃ ἔστι,
λάθρῃ Ἀχιλλῆος θρασὺν Ἕκτορα·
sentences.l:
But, truly, we shall let the stealing go, nor is it in any way possible,
in secret from Achilles, to steal bold Hector;
sentences.i: But as for stealing, we shall let that go, for there is no way, in secret from Achilles, to steal bold Hector;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἤτοι ‘but truly’. κλέψαι μὲν ἐάσομεν is ‘we shall let stealing be’, with ἐάσομεν a future of ἐάω ‘let, leave’ and κλέψαι an aorist infinitive; οὐδέ πῃ ἔστι is ‘nor is there any way’, ἔστι standing as ‘it is possible’. λάθρῃ Ἀχιλλῆος is ‘secretly from Achilles’, and θρασὺν Ἕκτορα ‘bold Hector’ is the object of a κλέψαι ‘to steal’ understood from the first clause. The unit ends in the middle of line 72.

sentences.t:
ἦ γάρ οἱ αἰεὶ
μήτηρ παρμέμβλωκεν ὁμῶς νύκτάς τε καὶ ἦμαρ.
sentences.l:
for in truth his mother always
stays by him, alike nights and day.
sentences.i: for his mother is always at his side, by night and by day alike.
sentences.n: ἦ γάρ ‘for in truth’ explains why stealing cannot work. παρμέμβλωκεν is a perfect, ‘has come to be beside and stays’, of a rare verb for coming alongside, and its sense here is ‘is at his side’; οἱ is ‘to him’. νύκτας and ἦμαρ are accusatives of time, ‘nights’ and ‘day’, and ὁμῶς means ‘equally’. The unit begins in the middle of line 72.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ εἴ τις καλέσειε θεῶν Θέτιν ἆσσον ἐμεῖο,
sentences.l: But if one of the gods would call Thetis nearer to me,
sentences.i: But if only one of the gods would call Thetis nearer to me,
sentences.n: εἴ τις καλέσειε is ‘if someone would call’, an optative with εἰ that is used as a wish; the main clause is not given, and the purpose clause in 75 takes its place. τις … θεῶν is ‘one of the gods’, and ἆσσον ἐμεῖο is ‘nearer to me’, ἆσσον being a comparative with the genitive.

sentences.t:
ὄφρά τί οἱ εἴπω πυκινὸν ἔπος, ὥς κεν Ἀχιλλεὺς
δώρων ἐκ Πριάμοιο λάχῃ ἀπό θ’ Ἕκτορα λύσῃ.
sentences.l:
so that I may say to her some shrewd word, how Achilles
may take gifts from Priam and release Hector.”
sentences.i: so that I may say a shrewd word to her, so that Achilles may take gifts from Priam and release Hector.”
sentences.n: ὄφρα with the subjunctive εἴπω says ‘so that I may say’, and οἱ is ‘to her’, Thetis; πυκινὸν ἔπος is ‘a shrewd word’. ὥς κεν with the subjunctive is a second purpose clause, ‘so that Achilles may’: λάχῃ is an aorist subjunctive of λαγχάνω ‘obtain’, taking δώρων ἐκ Πριάμοιο ‘gifts from Priam’, and ἀπό … λύσῃ is a split verb (tmesis) for ἀπολύω ‘release’, with Ἕκτορα as the object. The closing quotation mark ends Zeus’s speech, which began at 65.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, ὦρτο δὲ Ἶρις ἀελλόπος ἀγγελέουσα,
sentences.l: So he spoke, and rose up Iris, storm-footed, to tell the news,
sentences.i: So Zeus spoke, and storm-footed Iris set out to bring news,
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ ‘so he spoke’ closes Zeus’s speech, and ὦρτο is the aorist middle of ὄρνυμι ‘rise, set out’. Ἶρις ἀελλόπος is ‘storm-footed Iris’: ἀελλόπος is built from ἄελλα ‘storm’ and πούς ‘foot’, though the second part is not quite certain. ἀγγελέουσα ‘to tell the news’ is a future participle, expressing purpose. The unit ends at the comma that ends line 77, and the same first line stands at 8.409.

sentences.t:
μεσσηγὺς δὲ Σάμου τε καὶ Ἴμβρου παιπαλοέσσης
ἔνθορε μείλανι πόντῳ·
sentences.l:
and between Samos and rugged Imbros
she leapt into the black sea;
sentences.i: and between Samos and rugged Imbros she leapt into the black sea;
sentences.n: μεσσηγύς ‘between’ takes two genitives, Σάμου and Ἴμβρου. Σάμος here is the Thracian island, not the large Samos off Ionia, and παιπαλοέσσης ‘rugged’ agrees with Ἴμβρου. ἔνθορε is an aorist of ἐνθρῴσκω ‘leap in’, and μείλανι πόντῳ is ‘to the black sea’, in a dative of motion, μείλανι being a lengthened form of μέλανι. The unit ends in the middle of line 79.

sentences.t: ἐπεστονάχησε δὲ λίμνη.
sentences.l: and the water groaned.
sentences.i: and the water groaned.
sentences.n: ἐπεστονάχησε is an aorist of ἐπιστοναχέω ‘groan loudly (in answer)’, and λίμνη is usually a standing pool, but here it is the sea Iris has hit; the English keeps ‘water’, as elsewhere for this word. The unit begins in the middle of line 79.

sentences.t: ἣ δὲ μολυβδαίνῃ ἰκέλη ἐς βυσσὸν ὄρουσεν,
sentences.l: and she, like a lead weight, rushed into the depth,
sentences.i: and she plunged into the deep like a lead weight,
sentences.n: ἣ δέ ‘and she’ is Iris. μολυβδαίνῃ is a lead weight, built on μόλυβδος ‘lead’, and ἰκέλη ‘like’ agrees with ἣ and takes it in the dative; ὄρουσεν is an aorist of ὀρούω ‘rush’, and ἐς βυσσόν is ‘into the depth’.

sentences.t:
ἥ τε κατ’ ἀγραύλοιο βοὸς κέρας ἐμβεβαυῖα
ἔρχεται ὠμηστῇσιν ἐπ’ ἰχθύσι κῆρα φέρουσα.
sentences.l:
which, set fast down along the horn of a field-dwelling ox,
goes to the raw-feeding fish, bringing death-fate.
sentences.i: which goes down along the horn of an ox of the fields, bringing death to the fish that feed on raw flesh.
sentences.n: ἥ τε ‘which’ starts the comparison, so ἥ is the lead weight. κατὰ … βοὸς κέρας is ‘down along the horn of the ox’, with ἀγραύλοιο ‘of the field’; ἐμβεβαυῖα is a perfect participle of ἐμβαίνω ‘step on, be set in’, so the weight stands in or on the horn. ἔρχεται ‘goes’ takes ἐπ’ ἰχθύσι ‘to the fish’, and ὠμηστῇσιν ‘raw-feeding’ describes them. κῆρα is the death-fate that the weight brings, and φέρουσα ‘bringing’ is a participle.

sentences.t: εὗρε δ’ ἐνὶ σπῆϊ γλαφυρῷ Θέτιν,
sentences.l: And she found Thetis in the hollow cave,
sentences.i: And she found Thetis in the hollow cave,
sentences.n: εὗρε is an aorist of εὑρίσκω ‘find’, and σπῆϊ is the dative of σπέος ‘cave’, with γλαφυρῷ ‘hollow’. The unit ends in the middle of line 83.

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δ’ ἄρ’ ἄλλαι
εἵαθ’ ὁμηγερέες ἅλιαι θεαί·
sentences.l:
and about her the others
sat, gathered together, the goddesses of the sea;
sentences.i: and about her sat the other sea-goddesses, gathered together;
sentences.n: ἀμφί here is an adverb, ‘about her’; ἄλλαι is ‘the others’ and ἅλιαι is ‘of the sea’ (from ἅλς ‘salt, sea’, a different word from ἅλιος ‘in vain’ in 92). εἵαθ’ is εἵατο, a past tense of ἧμαι ‘sit’, and ὁμηγερέες ‘gathered together’ agrees with ἄλλαι. The unit begins and ends in the middle of lines.

sentences.t:
ἣ δ’ ἐνὶ μέσσῃς
κλαῖε μόρον οὗ παιδὸς ἀμύμονος, ὅς οἱ ἔμελλε
φθίσεσθ’ ἐν Τροίῃ ἐριβώλακι τηλόθι πάτρης.
sentences.l:
and she in the midst of them
wept for the doom of her own blameless child, who was
to perish in rich-soiled Troy, far from his fatherland.
sentences.i: while she in the midst of them wept for the doom of her own blameless son, who was to perish in Troy of the rich soil, far from his native land.
sentences.n: ἣ δέ ‘and she’ is Thetis, and ἐνὶ μέσσῃς ‘in the middle’ is feminine plural, ‘in the midst of them’. κλαῖε ‘wept’ takes μόρον ‘doom’ as object (‘wept for’), and οὗ is ‘her own’. ὅς οἱ ἔμελλε ‘who was to’ is followed by φθίσεσθ’ ‘perish’, a future infinitive; οἱ is ‘for her’. ἐριβώλακι is ‘rich-soiled’, and τηλόθι πάτρης is ‘far from his fatherland’. The unit begins in the middle of line 84.

sentences.t: ἀγχοῦ δ’ ἱσταμένη προσέφη πόδας ὠκέα Ἶρις·
sentences.l: And standing close by, swift-in-feet Iris spoke;
sentences.i: Iris, swift of foot, came and stood close by, and spoke;
sentences.n: ἀγχοῦ ‘close by’ and ἱσταμένη ‘standing’ (the feminine participle of ἵσταμαι) belong to Iris, who has come to the cave. προσέφη is the past tense of πρόσφημι ‘speak to’; the person addressed is Thetis, named in the next unit. πόδας ὠκέα is ‘swift in feet’, an accusative of respect.

sentences.t: ὄρσο Θέτι· καλέει Ζεὺς ἄφθιτα μήδεα εἰδώς.
sentences.l: “Rise, Thetis; Zeus calls you, who knows counsels that never fail.”
sentences.i: “Rise, Thetis; Zeus is calling you, who knows counsels that never fail.”
sentences.n: ὄρσο is the aorist imperative middle of ὄρνυμι ‘rise up’, and Θέτι is the vocative. καλέει is the uncontracted form of καλεῖ, ‘calls’. μήδεα εἰδώς is ‘knowing counsels’, with ἄφθιτα ‘unfailing’ agreeing with μήδεα. The quotation marks open and close Iris’s one-line speech.

sentences.t: τὴν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα θεὰ Θέτις ἀργυρόπεζα·
sentences.l: Her then answered the goddess, silver-footed Thetis:
sentences.i: Then the goddess Thetis, silver-footed, answered her:
sentences.n: ἠμείβετ’ is an imperfect of ἀμείβομαι ‘answer’, and τὴν is ‘her’, Iris. ἀργυρόπεζα is ‘silver-footed’, Thetis’s stock epithet, and θεά ‘goddess’ stands with her name. The colon opens Thetis’s speech, which runs to 92.

sentences.t: τίπτέ με κεῖνος ἄνωγε μέγας θεός;
sentences.l: “Why ever does that great god bid me?
sentences.i: “Why does that great god bid me come?
sentences.n: τίπτε is τί ποτε ‘why ever’, and κεῖνος ‘that one’ with μέγας θεός ‘great god’ is Zeus. ἄνωγε ‘bids’ is a perfect with a present sense, and the Greek gives it no infinitive, so ‘come’ is understood from Iris’s message. The unit ends in the middle of line 90.

sentences.t:
αἰδέομαι δὲ
μίσγεσθ’ ἀθανάτοισιν,
sentences.l:
and I am ashamed
to mingle with the immortals,
sentences.i: and I am ashamed to mingle with the immortals,
sentences.n: αἰδέομαι ‘I am ashamed’ here takes an infinitive, μίσγεσθ’ ‘to mingle’, with ἀθανάτοισιν ‘with the immortals’ in the dative; μίσγεσθ’ is μίσγεσθαι with the last syllable elided. The unit begins in the middle of line 90.

sentences.t:
ἔχω δ’ ἄχε’ ἄκριτα θυμῷ.
εἶμι μέν, οὐδ’ ἅλιον ἔπος ἔσσεται ὅττί κεν εἴπῃ.
sentences.l:
and I have griefs, unsorted, in my heart.
I shall go, indeed, and not in vain will be the word, whatever he may say.”
sentences.i: and I have endless griefs in my heart. I will go; and whatever he says will not be a vain word.”
sentences.n: ἔχω ‘I have’ takes ἄχε’ ἄκριτα, the accusative plural of ἄχος ‘grief’ and of ἄκριτος ‘unsorted’, so ‘griefs that cannot be told apart or ended’; θυμῷ is ‘in heart’. The unit begins in the middle of line 91. εἶμι ‘I shall go’ is a present with future sense, and μέν looks forward to οὐδ’ ‘and not’. ἅλιον ἔπος is ‘a vain word’, with ἅλιος ‘in vain’ a different word from ἅλιαι ‘of the sea’ in 84; ὅττί κεν εἴπῃ is ‘whatever he may say’. The closing quotation mark ends Thetis’s one speech, which began at 90.
